move at all, and if you use Uber Eats (or your favorite food delivery app)
someone will literally bring you as many calories as you like! Our food
environment is a cornucopia of processed convenience snacks and calorie-
dense foods. There are numerous benefits to our modern convenience
society (don’t get me wrong, I love Netflix as much as the next person), but
unfortunately a major pitfall for health is that we’ve completely severed the
connection between energy expenditure and food acquisition. Convenience
is nice, but it’s coming at a high health cost. In our modern environment,
sugary and processed snacks light up areas of the brain that trigger the
dopamine reward system, driving us to consume more and more, an
evolutionary hangover from our past that leads to constant snacking, caloric
excess, and worsening health. It’s not just a game of willpower. Willpower
is finite; the processed-food environment is seemingly infinite.
Another problem is that processed food is literally everywhere. You
can’t go to a school, hospital, sports complex, or office without running into
processed foods. Senior investigator at the National Institute of Diabetes
and Digestive and Kidney Diseases in the United States Kevin Hall, PhD, is
currently investigating how processed foods impact health, rates of obesity,
and type 2 diabetes. It’s a really interesting question—did our food
environment cause the obesity epidemic? Dr. Hall has started to dissect this
dilemma from many different angles. Did a specific macronutrient lead to
the obesity epidemic? Is it really all about carbohydrates? Probably not,
says Dr. Hall. He highlights food availability in the US per capita has
